catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.4.1.1-2.4.1.2 (p. 26) and §2.4.4 'Is pitch in Dom genuine tone?' (pp. 31-33, Table 2.4)
catalog_quote: The examples above demonstrate that there are three basic pitch patterns for words regardless of the number of syllables. ... As can be seen above, if we assume that in Dom there are basically three pitch patterns regardless of the number of syllables, even though there are differences in realization due to phonological conditions, what contrast can be interpreted not as tones in the sense of the pitch of each syllable, but as pitch patterns which have words as their domain. (74) tones: high (H), falling (HL), rising (LH) ... In this distinction, the definition of tone is based on whether the domain of the prosodic feature is a syllable or a word, which is a larger unit than a syllable. Then, from this standpoint the system of Dom is not 'tone' but a word-pitch system. audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (tonal: word-tone system with three lexical melodies H/HL/LH, no stress accent, no positional accent) rests on the authoritative source -- the fieldworker's 309-pp 2006 reference grammar with a full autosegmental tone chapter -- and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated sections/pages in the full text we hold. 'stress' occurs in the grammar only in the cross-linguistic typology (Russian), never for Dom. The official Japanese thesis abstract (held) and Tida 2013 on the second Dom dialect (downloaded now, open, Kumamoto repository) independently restate word-domain phonemic tone with three melodies. No instrumental study, JIPA illustration, or later phonology article on Dom exists in Glottolog, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, CiNii, J-STAGE or the author's researchmap list; the only unheld descriptive item is the author's own 2000 MA thesis, superseded. sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: ドム語には語彙的・辨別的な語を単位とするピッチ・パタンがある。メロディーは高型、下降型、上昇型が區別される、音素的な聲調（トーン）である。[Dom has lexical, distinctive pitch patterns with the word as unit; melodies high, falling, rising are distinguished; it is phonemic tone.] Dom 1 further splits rising into A (first syllable always low) and B (first-syllable pitch unspecified, some verb futures only); Dom 2 has the same melodies but the A/B distinction is less clear, with optional initial H on longer/heavy-syllable words. No stress or accent-location statement.
